name: Marco Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Marco, thanks for your time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I do marketing for Ridgeline, an outdoor gear brand that sells bike lights, bags and rain jackets online. Most of my day is email campaigns and product launches: I plan who gets what email, write it, test two versions, and check the results by the afternoon. I've built a little chain of AI tools that drafts the first versions and sorts the customer list, so I spend more time thinking than typing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the testing. Sending two subject lines and watching which one wins by lunchtime is like a tiny horse race. What drains me is that I'm on low pay for what I do, and Lena, my partner, works behind a bar with hours that change every week. Between us we've got less than a month saved, and there are maybe three firms in this town that hire people like me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do AI tools feature in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all day. I was the first in the office to try them, and now I'm the one people ask when theirs breaks. I don't think that makes me safe, though. I think it just means I can see the wave earlier than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. So all my little tool chains turn out to be a nice hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not magic, and anyone who said otherwise was selling something. I'd still post my tips online, because saving an hour a day is still an hour. I'd probably joke that I backed the wrong horse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit deflated, because I bet my edge on this. My job's fine, but it's a low-paid job in a town with three employers, and that was the problem before AI. Lena's winter hours always drop, so January is always tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the same way, with the tools saving me time. I'd use that spare hour to build up freelance work: email set-ups for small shops around town, for a couple of hundred each. And I'd put every freelance payment straight into savings until we've got two months, not three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit flat, like a party that ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which shops would you go to first for freelance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a bakery on Mill Street with a queue out the door and no email list at all, and a bike repair place that still uses a paper diary. I already know both owners from buying stuff there. I'd offer them a first month free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said January is always tight. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's hours halve after New Year, so we eat a lot of lentils and skip the heating in the bedroom. We've never missed rent, but we've been a day from it. That's the bit that never makes the news.

I'd keep sharing **time-saving tips** online, and joke I backed the wrong horse.
think: I think my **job's fine**, but the **low pay** was always the problem.
Lena's **winter hours** drop every year, so January is always tight.
do: Keep using the tools to **save an hour** a day at Ridgeline.
Sell **email set-ups** to small local shops for a couple of hundred each.
Put every **freelance payment** into savings until we reach two months.
feel: I feel **fine, mostly**, but a bit **flat**.
S0.quote: We've never missed rent, but we've been a day from it.

His real pressure is **low pay** and a partner with unsteady hours.

steps.text: Keep running the AI email drafts at Ridgeline to save time
Offer the Mill Street bakery a free first month of emails
Put every freelance payment into savings until two months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I actually expect, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say the gains have to be shared: if AI does half the work, give people a four-day week, not a pink slip. I'd post about it and try to get people at work talking. I'd also say, learn the tools, because that's your best protection right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who stays, because I'm the one who built the tools. But staying might mean doing three people's work for my same low pay. And if Ridgeline cuts the two others in marketing, they've nowhere to go in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who runs AI for the whole marketing side, and ask for a pay rise to match, in writing. I'd push for a staff group to bargain over a four-day week. I'd keep growing the freelance work, maybe five small clients by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm probably okay, but I'm watching friends who aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who does our social posts. She's brilliant with people, but she hates the tools and says so in meetings. I'd sit with her and show her the three things that would save her job, if she let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ridgeline says no to the pay rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go freelance part-time and make the rise myself. With five clients at a couple of hundred each, that's a real second income. It's not ideal, but it's better than doing three jobs for one wage.

I'd tell people to **learn the tools** as their best protection.

S1.quote: If AI does half the work, give people a four-day week, not a pink slip.
fieldNote: He expects to be **kept** and frames his worry around fairness and pay.

steps.text: Run AI tools for all of Ridgeline's marketing and ask for a rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That one actually scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that governments need to get money to people fast: a basic income, paid for by taxing the firms that profit. I'd organise, not just post. I'd tell everyone I know to stop assuming their job is the exception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, being good with AI tools stops mattering once AI doesn't need me to drive it. By 2028, Ridgeline's marketing could be run by one manager and a subscription. My freelance clients wouldn't need me either, they'd just ask the AI themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every penny out of the two years: sell AI set-ups to every small business in town while they still need a person to help. I'd save half of whatever that brings. Then I'd look hard at hands-on work, because robots only come around 2031. And I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like being the first person to see the smoke, and still not getting out in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bike repairs, honestly. I've fixed my own bikes since I was twelve, and Ridgeline sells to people who ride. It would buy me three years, maybe more, before a robot can true a wheel as well as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Lena manage on the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, for a while. Bar work is hands-on too, so Lena might be the steadier one for once. We'd stop thinking about a bigger flat and just hold on to this one.

say: I'd demand a **basic income**, paid by taxing firms that profit.
I'd **organise**, not just post, and warn everyone no job is the exception.
think: I think my **AI skills stop mattering** once AI needs no driver.

do: Sell **AI set-ups** to every local business while they still need help.

feel: I feel **alarmed**, like seeing smoke first and still not **getting out**.
S2.quote: Being good with AI tools stops mattering once AI doesn't need me to drive it.
fieldNote: Fast AGI cancels his main advantage: **driving the tools**.
He sees **bike repair** as a three-year hands-on bridge.
His partner's **bar work** may become the steadier income.

steps.text: Sell AI set-ups to every small business in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to build something, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to set up the safety net, while there's time. I'd push our town's council to fund retraining and get people talking about a basic income before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got about four good years in marketing, and I should use them. The thinking side of my work goes in 2031, but robots don't reach bike workshops until about 2034, so I could plan a move instead of scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and run AI for the whole team, saving every bit of the extra. I'd take a weekend bike mechanic course this year and start doing repairs for friends. By year three I'd want to talk to the repair shop owner, Tom, about going in with him. And I'd keep pushing the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the useful way. I've got a map, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Going in with Tom would take money. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the weak bit. Maybe a small loan, maybe Tom lets me buy in slowly from my wages. I won't have a big lump, so I'd have to make myself useful enough that he wants me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Lena have a say in this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have the biggest say. She's told me before she'd rather I was happy with oil on my hands than stressed at a laptop. I think she'd like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like a long game I could actually play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so no excuses: share the gains, shorten the week, fund retraining. I'd be one of the people organising at work and in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could ride marketing for six or seven years and do well, because I'm good with these tools. But I'd be stupid to pretend the end point is different. I'd want something real built before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard at Ridgeline for a better title and pay, since I'd be the AI person for years. I'd learn bike mechanics slowly, at weekends. I'd save toward buying into a repair shop, and maybe start a little repair stall at the market on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. Ten years is a lot of time to get ready, and also a lot of time to get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you say get lazy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when you're doing well, you don't want to start again. I've seen people wait too long. I'd have to set myself a date, like 2032, and stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lena make different plans with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd maybe think about kids, which we've not dared to. Ten years feels like enough time to have a plan for them. With two years, we wouldn't even talk about it.

I'd **organise** at work and in town.
think: I think I could **ride marketing** for six or seven years.
The **end point** doesn't change, so I'd build something before 2036.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My one advantage disappears and I've got three weeks of money. What would help is a basic income, even a small one, so people can retrain without losing their homes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who love these tools. Everyone assumes we're relaxed. Some of us who love these tools are just closer to the edge, so we see it better.

headlineQuote: Some of us who love these tools are just closer to the edge, so we see it better.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old email marketer** at an outdoor gear brand who uses AI tools every day.
He's on **low pay**, with a bartender partner and under a month saved.
He leans left and wants **shared gains**, a four-day week and a basic income.
He's **uneasy** in the milder pictures but **alarmed** by AGI in two years.
His plan B is **bike repair**, a hands-on trade he has done since childhood.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his AI advantage disappears and he has three weeks of money.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income**, even a small one, so people can retrain without losing homes.
